newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces up to surgery, aides look ahead.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces up to surgery, aides look ahead.

text.p: Russian Boris Yeltsin has put a brave face on the prospect of undergoing heart surgery at the end of the month, but the minds of Kremlin insiders are already focused on who will take his place.

Yeltsin, who dropped out of sight in July, ended months of speculation on the issue of his failing health to tell Russians on Thursday that he had decided to have the operation, which doctors later said would be a bypass.

"Passive work has never suited me," Yeltsin, 65, said in a rare television interview. "Nor can it suit me now. That's why an operation and full recovery, as they promise, is better for me than passive activity, passive work."

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who visited the Kremlin leader, a personal friend, at his hunting lodge outside Moscow on Saturday said Yeltsin was "very optimistic" about the surgery which comes just two months into his second term.

Interfax news agency said Yeltsin had bagged more than 40 ducks and a hefty wild boar over the past week, adding to the impression of vigour evident from the television pictures of a relaxed-looking president strolling with Kohl.

Troops began their first withdrawals from rebel Chechnya on Sunday under a peace deal meant to resolve the biggest problem of Yeltsin's rule. But doubts over that deal only served to underline the power vacuum at the top of Russian politics.

Cheerful military music accompanied a withdrawal ceremony from a Russian base near the Chechen capital Grozny. But the atmosphere was muted by the army's humiliation during 21 months of inconclusive warfare in which tens of thousands have died.
It is still not clear how many other soldiers will follow those of the 133rd battalion in heading for home and whether the separatists will simply grab power if they all go.

Security chief Alexander Lebed signed the deal with the rebels but he has expressed concern that he has not had full support from Yeltsin, who has questioned the early withdrawal of troops from the separatist North Caucasus region.

Lebed said on Friday Yeltsin should let Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin take over until he recovered. But the president's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais said he did not need to step down yet. The three men are part of an uneasy power triangle.
Under Russia's constitution the prime minister takes over if the president is incapacitated, but it does not specify the conditions or procedure for the handover.

Lebed hinted that the jostling for position had already gone a step further behind the scenes, agreeing with a suggestion by the German magazine Der Spiegel that Kremlin insiders were already looking to the post-Yeltsin era.

"It is against our customs to talk about an older person as if he is no longer there, in particular because he is still the president of our nation and was just recently re-elected. But you could nevertheless be quite correct with your Kremlin prognosis," it quoted him as saying.
Yeltsin, who fought off a communist challenger in July with an energetic election campaign, appeared to have no plans to give up power yet.

He told Kohl, the first Western leader to meet him since the election, that he would play an active role in settling Russia's dispute with NATO over the alliance's plans to admit former Soviet-bloc countries in eastern Europe.
Kohl said Yeltsin, who the West openly supported in the election campaign as a guarantor of stability and market reforms, was on good form.
"President Yeltsin was fully active throughout these discussions," he said. "Boris Yeltsin is very optimistic that this procedure, which is essential...will be successful."
